claim: Multiple NGATHA (NGA) and CINCINNATA-class-TCP (CIN-TCP) transcription factors act redundantly, shortly after leaf initiation, to gradually restrict the activity of a leaf meristem in Arabidopsis thaliana to marginal and basal domains.
source: Here we demonstrate that multiple NGATHA (NGA) and CINCINNATA-class-TCP (CIN-TCP) transcription factors act redundantly, shortly after leaf initiation, to gradually restrict the activity of a leaf meristem in Arabidopsis thaliana to marginal and basal domains
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that reduction of NGA and CIN-TCP activities results in persistent marginal growth, as demonstrated through genetic manipulation and marker expression analysis.

claim: The absence of NGA and CIN-TCP transcription factors confers persistent marginal growth to leaves, cotyledons and floral organs.
source: and that their absence confers persistent marginal growth to leaves, cotyledons and floral organs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the phenotypes observed in 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants showing continuous de novo formation of tissue at the margins of all lateral organs.

claim: Following primordia initiation, the restriction of the broadly acting leaf meristem to the margins is mediated by the juxtaposition of adaxial and abaxial domains.
source: Following primordia initiation, the restriction of the broadly acting leaf meristem to the margins is mediated by the juxtaposition of adaxial and abaxial domains and maintained by WOX homeobox transcription factors
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that radialized phb-1d/+ leaves without adaxial-abaxial juxtaposition do not exhibit marginal growth even when NGA and CIN-TCP activities are reduced.

claim: The leaf meristem is maintained by WOX homeobox transcription factors.
source: Following primordia initiation, the restriction of the broadly acting leaf meristem to the margins is mediated by the juxtaposition of adaxial and abaxial domains and maintained by WOX homeobox transcription factors
evidence: The prs wox1 double mutants suppressed the indeterminate marginal growth in 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants, demonstrating the requirement of WOX genes for ongoing leaf margin growth.

claim: Other marginal elaboration genes are dispensable for maintenance of the leaf meristem.
source: whereas other marginal elaboration genes are dispensable for its maintenance.
evidence: The cotyledon and/or leaf margins continue to grow in cuc2 cuc3 and cuc1 cuc2 mutants expressing the 35S:miR319a-amiR-NGA transgene, indicating that continued margin growth is independent of CUC-mediated marginal elaboration.

claim: This genetic framework parallels the morphogenetic program of shoot apical meristems.
source: This genetic framework parallels the morphogenetic program of shoot apical meristems and may represent a relic of an ancestral shoot system from which seed plant leaves evolved.
evidence: The parallel is inferred from the shared use of WOX genes and adaxial/abaxial polarity factors in both shoot and leaf meristems.

claim: The leaf meristem genetic framework may represent a relic of an ancestral shoot system from which seed plant leaves evolved.
source: This genetic framework parallels the morphogenetic program of shoot apical meristems and may represent a relic of an ancestral shoot system from which seed plant leaves evolved.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on fossil evidence and the observation that seed plant leaves evolved from ancestral shoot systems.

claim: Anatomical features typical of apical or vascular meristems are not present in leaves.
source: However, as anatomical features typical of apical or vascular meristems are not present in leaves, whether developing leaves grow from a localized meristem has been debated for nearly a century (Foster, 1936; Hagemann and Gleissberg, 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from historical literature.

claim: Whether developing leaves grow from a localized meristem has been debated for nearly a century.
source: However, as anatomical features typical of apical or vascular meristems are not present in leaves, whether developing leaves grow from a localized meristem has been debated for nearly a century (Foster, 1936; Hagemann and Gleissberg, 1996).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citations.

claim: Caspar Wolff described the leaf lamina arising from the margins of Brassica 'capitata' (cabbage) leaves.
source: In one of the first detailed examinations of development at the plant shoot apex Caspar Wolff described the leaf lamina arising from the margins of Brassica 'capitata' (cabbage) leaves (Wolff, 1759).
evidence: This is a historical observation cited from Wolff's work.

claim: Avery suggested that early lamina growth of Nicotiana tabaccum was initiated by a row of subepidermal initial cells located at the upper-lower (adaxial-abaxial) leaf boundary that he termed the 'marginal meristem'.
source: Subsequently, Avery suggested that early lamina growth of Nicotiana tabaccum was initiated by a row of subepidermal initial cells located at the upper-lower (adaxial-abaxial) leaf boundary that he termed the 'marginal meristem' (Avery, 1933).
evidence: This is a historical observation cited from Avery's work.

claim: Later protracted growth in leaves occurs in tissues that are not marginal, but rather within the developing lamina in a region described as a 'plate meristem'.
source: However, it had already been noted that later protracted growth in leaves occurs in tissues that are not marginal, but rather within the developing lamina in a region described as a 'plate meristem' (Schüepp, 1918, 1926).
evidence: This is a historical observation cited from Schüepp's work.

claim: Early views of leaf development were perceived to consist of two growth phases.
source: Thus, early views of leaf development were perceived to consist of two growth phases (Foster, 1936).
evidence: This is a historical perspective cited from Foster's work.

claim: An early ephemeral phase of cell divisions without cell expansion produces the characteristic 6–10 cell layers of the leaf thickness via submarginal periclinal cell divisions and epidermal anticlinal divisions.
source: An early ephemeral phase of cell divisions without cell expansion produces the characteristic 6–10 cell layers of the leaf thickness via submarginal periclinal cell divisions and epidermal anticlinal divisions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about leaf development.

claim: A later prolonged growth phase produces the bulk of two-dimensional lamina growth via a plate meristem in which cell divisions are predominantly anticlinal.
source: This is followed by a later prolonged growth phase where the bulk of two-dimensional lamina growth is produced via a plate meristem in which cell divisions are predominantly anticlinal.
evidence: This is established knowledge about leaf development.

claim: Analyses of leaf development in the middle of the 20th century sought to identify patterns of submarginal cell divisions to identify initial cells, but the patterns of cell division were highly variable between species casting doubt on the presence of specific initials.
source: Analyses of leaf development in the middle of the 20th century sought to identify patterns of submarginal cell divisions to identify initial cells, but the patterns of cell division were highly variable between species casting doubt on the presence of specific initials (Foster, 1936).
evidence: This is a historical observation cited from Foster's work.

claim: A higher rate of cell division is observed in submarginal (i.e. plate meristem) regions of the leaf as compared to the margins.
source: More recently, examination of mitotic indices during leaf development revealed that a higher rate of cell division is observed in submarginal (i.e. plate meristem) regions of the leaf as compared to the margins (Maksymowych and Erickson, 1960; Fuchs, 1966; Thomasson, 1970; Dubuc-Lebreux and Sattler, 1981; Jéune, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies on mitotic indices.

claim: Sector analysis of leaf development in several eudicot species, including N. tabacum, revealed that most clonal sectors were located between the midrib and the margin, with only a minority extending all the way to the margin.
source: Furthermore, sector analysis of leaf development in several eudicot species, including N. tabacum, revealed that most clonal sectors were located between the midrib and the margin, with only a minority extending all the way to the margin (Dulieu, 1968; Poethig and Sussex, 1985; Dolan and Poethig, 1998)
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited sector analysis studies.

claim: Leaves do not grow from the margins sensu stricto.
source: Furthermore, sector analysis of leaf development in several eudicot species, including N. tabacum, revealed that most clonal sectors were located between the midrib and the margin, with only a minority extending all the way to the margin (Dulieu, 1968; Poethig and Sussex, 1985; Dolan and Poethig, 1998), indicating that leaves do not grow from the margins sensu stricto, and calling into question the concept of the leaf marginal meristem.
evidence: This is an inference from sector analysis data.

claim: The defining features of meristems are their organogenetic potential and cytohistological state rather than specific cell division patterns.
source: However, noting the overall lack of organized cell division patterns in plants, Hagemann and Gleissberg argued that the defining features of meristems are their organogenetic potential and cytohistological state rather than specific cell division patterns.
evidence: This is a theoretical perspective cited from Hagemann and Gleissberg's work.

claim: The marginal meristem (or 'blastozone') is responsible for primary morphogenetic events, e.g. lamina initiation, but is used up early in leaf development, with most lamina expansion occurring during a later leaf differentiation phase.
source: Thus, in their view the marginal meristem (or 'blastozone', as they refer to it) is responsible for primary morphogenetic events, e.g. lamina initiation, but is used up early in leaf development, with most lamina expansion occurring during a later leaf differentiation phase (Hagemann and Gleissberg, 1996).
evidence: This is a theoretical model cited from Hagemann and Gleissberg's work.

claim: Removal of multiple growth suppressing transcriptional factors results in indeterminate growth of the margins of all lateral organs.
source: Here we show that removal of multiple growth suppressing transcriptional factors results in indeterminate growth of the margins of all lateral organs, coupled with sustained organogenesis and activity of gene modules shared amongst other plant meristems.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the phenotypes observed in 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants.

claim: Removal of multiple growth suppressing transcriptional factors results in sustained organogenesis and activity of gene modules shared amongst other plant meristems.
source: Here we show that removal of multiple growth suppressing transcriptional factors results in indeterminate growth of the margins of all lateral organs, coupled with sustained organogenesis and activity of gene modules shared amongst other plant meristems.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the continued expression of meristem markers like PRS, WOX1, and PIN1 in 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants.

claim: The finding supports the presence of a specific leaf meristem.
source: Our finding supports the presence of a specific leaf meristem, and conforms to the view stemming from the fossil record that recruitment of suppressors of meristematic activity was critical in seed plant leaf evolution and development.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing that removal of suppressors leads to persistent meristematic activity.

claim: Recruitment of suppressors of meristematic activity was critical in seed plant leaf evolution and development.
source: Our finding supports the presence of a specific leaf meristem, and conforms to the view stemming from the fossil record that recruitment of suppressors of meristematic activity was critical in seed plant leaf evolution and development.
evidence: This is an inference combining experimental data with evolutionary reasoning based on fossil evidence.

claim: In Arabidopsis, leaf morphogenesis is initiated at the flanks of the shoot apical meristem (SAM) where leaf primordia develop as flattened lamina with defined abaxial, adaxial and marginal cell types.
source: In Arabidopsis, leaf morphogenesis is initiated at the flanks of the shoot apical meristem (SAM) where leaf primordia develop as flattened lamina with defined abaxial, adaxial and marginal cell types (Tsukaya, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Tsukaya's work.

claim: Lamina development requires the juxtaposition of abaxial/adaxial polarity factors, including adaxial class III HD-Zip and abaxial KANADI transcription factors.
source: Lamina development requires the juxtaposition of abaxial/adaxial polarity factors, including adaxial class III HD-Zip and abaxial KANADI transcription factors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about leaf development.

claim: Abaxial/adaxial polarity factors lie on either side of a narrow middle domain expressing the WUSCHEL RELATED HOMEOBOX (WOX) genes, PRESSED FLOWER (PRS) and WOX1, and together promote organ growth and differentiation.
source: These lie on either side of a narrow middle domain expressing the WUSCHEL RELATED HOMEOBOX (WOX) genes, PRESSED FLOWER (PRS) and WOX1, and together promote organ growth and differentiation (Nakata et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2011; Eshed et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple studies.

claim: In Arabidopsis leaf development, expression of growth genes rapidly diminishes distally but can persist proximally.
source: In Arabidopsis leaf development, expression of growth genes rapidly diminishes distally but can persist proximally (Donnelly et al., 1999; Nath et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple studies.

claim: This proximo-distal differentiation gradient is regulated by CIN-TCP transcription factors.
source: This proximo-distal differentiation gradient is regulated by CIN-TCP transcription factors (Nath et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Nath et al.'s work.

claim: A reduction of five CIN-TCPs targeted by the endogenous microRNA, miR319a (also known as miR-JAW) results in delayed basipetal progression of a mitotic arrest front and increased cell proliferation particularly at leaf margins, producing crinkly and serrated leaves.
source: A reduction of five CIN-TCPs targeted by the endogenous microRNA, miR319a (also known as miR-JAW) results in delayed basipetal progression of a mitotic arrest front and increased cell proliferation particularly at leaf margins, producing crinkly and serrated leaves (Efroni et al., 2008; Ori et al., 2007; Palatnik et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple studies.

claim: Increased distal leaf growth and serrations are observed when the activities of the four NGA transcription factors are reduced.
source: Increased distal leaf growth and serrations are also observed when the activities of the four NGA transcription factors are reduced (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Trigueros et al., 2009; Alvarez et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and cited studies.

claim: The NGAs and CIN-TCPs are co-expressed at many stages of leaf development, exemplified by the distal expression of TCP3, TCP4, NGA1 and NGA4 in young leaves.
source: The NGAs and CIN-TCPs are co-expressed at many stages of leaf development, exemplified by the distal expression of TCP3, TCP4, NGA1 and NGA4 in young leaves (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is demonstrated by expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: miR319 is expressed at the leaf base.
source: and in contrast to the reported expression of miR319 at the leaf base (Obayashi et al., 2009; Nag et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple studies.

claim: Similarities in loss-of-function phenotypes of NGAs and CIN-TCPs suggest shared roles in leaf development.
source: This, together with similarities in their loss-of-function phenotypes, suggests shared roles in leaf development.
evidence: This is an inference from observed phenotypic similarities.

claim: Simultaneous reduction in expression of nine genes (four NGAs and five CIN-TCPs) resulted in continuous de novo formation of tissue at the margins of all lateral organs including cotyledons, leaves and floral organs.
source: Strikingly, simultaneous reduction in expression of these nine genes resulted in continuous de novo formation of tissue at the margins of all lateral organs including cotyledons, leaves and floral organs (Figure 1A–B, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phenotypic data shown in Figure 1A–B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants grow more slowly, are later flowering, and their leaf margins harbor proliferative cell populations unlike those of 35S:amiR-NGA and 35S:miR319a singly transgenic plants.
source: 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants grow more slowly, are later flowering, and their leaf margins harbor proliferative cell populations unlike those of 35S:amiR-NGA and 35S:miR319a singly transgenic plants (Figure 1C–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 3–8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phenotypic and cellular data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Application of stain to 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA leaf margins indicates continued proliferation at the leaf margin, with the marker displaced sub-marginally over time.
source: Application of stain to 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA leaf margins indicates continued proliferation at the leaf margin, with the marker displaced sub-marginally over time (Figure 1D1–D2, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by marking experiments shown in Figure 1D1–D2.

claim: In 35S:miR319a nga1,2,3,4 or 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants, the entirety of the older leaf margin consists of small densely packed cells lacking chlorophyll, rather than the large, elongate cells characteristic of wild-type leaf margins.
source: In 35S:miR319a nga1,2,3,4 or 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants, the entirety of the older leaf margin consists of small densely packed cells lacking chlorophyll, rather than the large, elongate cells characteristic of wild-type leaf margins (Figure 1C–I, Figure 1—figure supplement 5–8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Sections of leaf primordia and differentiating leaves suggest that the six-cell-layered blade organization of young wild-type leaf primordia is maintained at 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA leaf margins.
source: Sections of leaf primordia and differentiating leaves suggest that the six-cell-layered blade organization of young wild-type leaf primordia is maintained at 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA leaf margins ([Nakata et al., 2012]; Figure 1E–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological sections shown in Figure 1E–G and Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: The digital differentiation index (DDI) of dissected, older 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA leaf margins clearly matches that of initiating primordia.
source: The digital differentiation index (DDI) assesses relative leaf maturity from global gene expression profiles (Efroni et al., 2008). The index of dissected, older 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA leaf margins clearly matches that of initiating primordia (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Expression of markers demonstrate ongoing leaf-primordium-like activity at the leaf margins of 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants.
source: This result is further supported by the expression of markers that highlight continued cell division, distinguishing epidermal nuclei (ATML1:H2B-mYFP), epidermal plasma membrane (ATML1:mCitrine-RCI2A), general cell division (CYCB1;1:GFP), initiating trichomes (highlighted by GL2:GFP) and stomatal lineage proliferation (TMM:GUS-GFP) (Figure 1K,L, Figure 1—figure supplement 7), which demonstrate ongoing leaf-primordium-like activity at the leaf margins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by marker expression data shown in Figure 1K,L and Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: In initiating wild-type leaves, auxin flux, marked by PINFORMED1 (PIN1) expression, converges at the distal tip and at serrations, where it inwardly canalizes leaf vascular development, before becoming restricted to proximal margins of older leaves.
source: In initiating wild-type leaves, auxin flux, marked by PINFORMED1 (PIN1) expression, converges at the distal tip and at serrations, where it inwardly canalizes leaf vascular development, before becoming restricted to proximal margins of older leaves (Bilsborough et al., 2011; Scarpella et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple studies.

claim: Compared to wild-type leaves, in both 35S:amiR-NGA and 35S:miR319a individual knockdown leaves auxin flux persists longer at distal leaf margins.
source: Compared to wild-type leaves, in both 35S:amiR-NGA and 35S:miR319a individual knockdown leaves auxin flux persists longer at distal leaf margins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by PIN1 expression data.

claim: In the 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA combined knockdown leaves, auxin flux continues around the entire leaf margin.
source: Strikingly, in the 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA combined knockdown leaves, auxin flux continues around the entire leaf margin (Figure 1O, Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PIN1 expression data shown in Figure 1O and Figure 1—figure supplement 9.

claim: Auxin canalization and ongoing de novo vasculature morphogenesis at 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA margins is marked by expression of the provascular makers ATHB8 and MONOPTEROS (MP).
source: Auxin canalization and ongoing de novo vasculature morphogenesis at these margins is marked by expression of the provascular makers ATHB8 and MONOPTEROS (MP) (Figure 1M–N, Figure 1—figure supplements 7 and 10).
evidence: This is demonstrated by marker expression data shown in Figure 1M–N and supplementary figures.

claim: The organ marginal markers PRS and WOX1 are transiently expressed in initiating wild-type leaves before becoming proximally restricted.
source: Paralleling marginal auxin flux, the organ marginal markers PRS and WOX1 are transiently expressed in initiating wild-type leaves before becoming proximally restricted.
evidence: This is demonstrated by marker expression data.

claim: When NGA or CIN-TCP activities are reduced, PRS and WOX1 distal expression persists in older leaves.
source: When NGA or CIN-TCP activities are reduced, PRS and WOX1 distal expression persists in older leaves
evidence: This is demonstrated by marker expression data.

claim: In the combined loss in 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA leaves PRS and WOX1 expression occurs in an uninterrupted marginal band.
source: whereas in the combined loss in 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA leaves PRS and WOX1 expression occurs in an uninterrupted marginal band, again suggesting that these margins retain meristematic properties equivalent to initiating leaf primordia (Figure 1P, Figure 1—figure supplements 11 and 12).
evidence: This is demonstrated by marker expression data shown in Figure 1P and supplementary figures.

claim: Expression of miR319a-amiR-NGA under control of the PRS regulatory sequences results in indeterminate margins.
source: That expression of miR319a-amiR-NGA under control of the PRS regulatory sequences results in indeterminate margins confirms that marginal loss of NGA and CIN-TCP activity is sufficient to allow the maintenance of these meristematic characteristics (Figure 1—figure supplement 13).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phenotypic data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 13.

claim: Marginal loss of NGA and CIN-TCP activity is sufficient to allow the maintenance of meristematic characteristics.
source: That expression of miR319a-amiR-NGA under control of the PRS regulatory sequences results in indeterminate margins confirms that marginal loss of NGA and CIN-TCP activity is sufficient to allow the maintenance of these meristematic characteristics (Figure 1—figure supplement 13).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the PRS>>miR319a-amiR-NGA experiment.

claim: The lamina away from the margins of PRS>>miR319a-amiR-NGA is thinner and more wild-type in appearance than that of 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA leaves.
source: Notably the lamina away from the margins of PRS>>miR319a-amiR-NGA is thinner and more wild-type in appearance than that of 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA leaves suggesting that the broader, non-marginal expression of the NGAs and CIN-TCPs may reflect an activity in regulating cell expansion that remains functional in PRS>>miR319a-amiR-NGA leaves (Figure 1—figure supplement 8 and Figure 1—figure supplement 13).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The broader, non-marginal expression of the NGAs and CIN-TCPs may reflect an activity in regulating cell expansion.
source: Notably the lamina away from the margins of PRS>>miR319a-amiR-NGA is thinner and more wild-type in appearance than that of 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA leaves suggesting that the broader, non-marginal expression of the NGAs and CIN-TCPs may reflect an activity in regulating cell expansion that remains functional in PRS>>miR319a-amiR-NGA leaves (Figure 1—figure supplement 8 and Figure 1—figure supplement 13).
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of PRS>>miR319a-amiR-NGA and 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA phenotypes.

claim: The extended maintenance of primordium identity was observed in the cotyledons of 35S:miR319a nga1,2,3,4 or 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants, which continuously produce tissue with leaf characteristics including stellate trichome formation.
source: The extended maintenance of primordium identity was also observed in the cotyledons of 35S:miR319a nga1,2,3,4 or 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants, which continuously produce tissue with leaf characteristics including stellate trichome formation (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 14).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phenotypic data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 14.

claim: Changes in the expression pattern of the cell division marker CYCB1;1:GFP are apparent in the distal embryonic cotyledons of 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants.
source: Changes in the expression pattern of the cell division marker CYCB1;1:GFP are apparent in the distal embryonic cotyledons while the respective expression of ATML1:H2B-mYFP and MONOPTEROS demonstrates the absence of the normal, marginal cell differentiation program and ectopic production of provascular strands implying an active marginal meristem similar to that observed in leaves (Figure 1—figure supplement 15).
evidence: This is demonstrated by marker expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 15.

claim: The expression of ATML1:H2B-mYFP and MONOPTEROS in 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA embryonic cotyledons demonstrates the absence of the normal, marginal cell differentiation program and ectopic production of provascular strands.
source: Changes in the expression pattern of the cell division marker CYCB1;1:GFP are apparent in the distal embryonic cotyledons while the respective expression of ATML1:H2B-mYFP and MONOPTEROS demonstrates the absence of the normal, marginal cell differentiation program and ectopic production of provascular strands implying an active marginal meristem similar to that observed in leaves (Figure 1—figure supplement 15).
evidence: This is demonstrated by marker expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 15.

claim: There was no evidence for impaired dormancy of 35S:miR319a nga1,2,3,4 or 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA seed.
source: Notably there was no evidence for impaired dormancy of 35S:miR319a nga1,2,3,4 or 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA seed suggesting that the seed-based program of imposed dormancy was as effective on this cotyledon marginal meristem as on the embryonic shoot and root meristems.
evidence: This is an observation from seed germination experiments.

claim: The seed-based program of imposed dormancy was as effective on the cotyledon marginal meristem as on the embryonic shoot and root meristems.
source: Notably there was no evidence for impaired dormancy of 35S:miR319a nga1,2,3,4 or 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA seed suggesting that the seed-based program of imposed dormancy was as effective on this cotyledon marginal meristem as on the embryonic shoot and root meristems.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that seed dormancy was not impaired.

claim: After germination, cotyledons of 35S:miR319a nga1,2,3,4 or 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA seedlings continue growth and express growth markers unlike wild-type.
source: After germination, cotyledons of 35S:miR319a nga1,2,3,4 or 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA seedlings continue growth and express growth markers unlike wild-type (Figure 1—figure supplements 14 and 15).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phenotypic and marker expression data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The floral organs of NGA and CIN-TCP compromised plants exhibit prolonged marginal growth.
source: The floral organs of NGA and CIN-TCP compromised plants also exhibit prolonged marginal growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phenotypic data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: NGA and CIN-TCP redundantly suppress marginal growth in all aerial lateral organs.
source: Hence NGA and CIN-TCP redundantly suppress marginal growth in all aerial lateral organs.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that all lateral organs show prolonged marginal growth when NGA and CIN-TCP activities are reduced.

claim: No evidence was found for the expression of meristem genes including SHOOT MERISTEMLESS (STM), WUSCHEL (WUS) and CLAVATA1/3 (CLV1/3) in indeterminate leaf margins of 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants.
source: We surveyed the expression of genes that are expressed in the SAM but not in leaves of Arabidopsis, and no evidence was found for the expression of meristem genes including SHOOT MERISTEMLESS (STM), WUSCHEL (WUS) and CLAVATA1/3 (CLV1/3) in indeterminate leaf margins of 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants (Figure 2A–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by expression analysis shown in Figure 2A–E.

claim: The 35S:miR319a-amiR-NGA transgene conferred indeterminate growth of cotyledon and/or leaf margins in stm-11 knat6-1 bp-9 triple and wus-1 single mutants where SAM activity is respectively lost or disrupted.
source: In agreement, the 35S:miR319a-amiR-NGA transgene conferred indeterminate growth of cotyledon and/or leaf margins in stm-11 knat6-1 bp-9 triple and wus-1 single mutants where SAM activity is respectively lost or disrupted (Figure 2F–L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phenotypic data shown in Figure 2F–L.

claim: Continued marginal growth in 35S:miR319a-amiR-NGA double knockdown leaves is not a consequence of secondarily acquiring characteristics of the indeterminate SAM.
source: Thus, continued marginal growth in 35S:miR319a-amiR-NGA double knockdown leaves is not a consequence of secondarily acquiring characteristics of the indeterminate SAM, as for example in YABBY-compromised mutants (Sarojam et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that SAM genes are not expressed and that the phenotype occurs even in SAM mutants.

claim: The NAC transcription factors CUP-SHAPED COTYLEDON2 (CUC2) and CUC3 are regulators of leaf margin shape in Arabidopsis and other angiosperm species.
source: The NAC transcription factors CUP-SHAPED COTYLEDON2 (CUC2) and CUC3 are regulators of leaf margin shape in Arabidopsis and other angiosperm species, and ectopic activation of CUC genes promotes adventitious shoot formation (Blein et al., 2008; Aichinger et al., 2012; Hibara et al., 2003)
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple studies.

claim: Ectopic activation of CUC genes promotes adventitious shoot formation.
source: The NAC transcription factors CUP-SHAPED COTYLEDON2 (CUC2) and CUC3 are regulators of leaf margin shape in Arabidopsis and other angiosperm species, and ectopic activation of CUC genes promotes adventitious shoot formation (Blein et al., 2008; Aichinger et al., 2012; Hibara et al., 2003)
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple studies.

claim: The cotyledon and/or leaf margins continue to grow in cuc2 cuc3 and cuc1 cuc2 mutants expressing the 35S:miR319a-amiR-NGA transgene.
source: However, we found that the cotyledon and/or leaf margins continue to grow in cuc2 cuc3 and cuc1 cuc2 mutants expressing the 35S:miR319a-amiR-NGA transgene.
evidence: This is demonstrated by phenotypic data.

claim: Continued margin growth is independent of CUC-mediated marginal elaboration.
source: This indicates that continued margin growth is independent of CUC-mediated marginal elaboration (Figure 2M–Q, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that the phenotype occurs in cuc mutants.

claim: The respective adaxial, marginal and abaxial genes PHABULOSA (PHB), PRS and KANADI1 (KAN1) are expressed in young, wild-type leaf primordia before diminishing in a basipetal fashion.
source: The respective adaxial, marginal and abaxial genes PHABULOSA (PHB), PRS and KANADI1 (KAN1) are expressed in young, wild-type leaf primordia before diminishing in a basipetal fashion (Figure 3A,C,E,G–H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by marker expression data shown in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claim: At the margins of 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA leaves, PHB, PRS and KAN1 gene expression continues indefinitely, with spatial relationships maintained.
source: At the margins of 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA leaves, PHB, PRS and KAN1 gene expression continues indefinitely, with spatial relationships maintained, implying that in older leaves with reduced CIN-TCP and NGA activities, the collective interplay among these genes is sustained as established in initiating wild-type leaf primordia (Figure 3A–H, Figure 1—figure supplement 11, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by marker expression data shown in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claim: In older leaves with reduced CIN-TCP and NGA activities, the collective interplay among PHB, PRS and KAN1 genes is sustained as established in initiating wild-type leaf primordia.
source: At the margins of 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA leaves, PHB, PRS and KAN1 gene expression continues indefinitely, with spatial relationships maintained, implying that in older leaves with reduced CIN-TCP and NGA activities, the collective interplay among these genes is sustained as established in initiating wild-type leaf primordia (Figure 3A–H, Figure 1—figure supplement 11, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference from the maintained expression patterns of polarity genes.

claim: Semi-dominant PHB alleles produce two leaf types on the same plant: partially radialized leaves with distal lamina and completely radialized (adaxialized) leaves.
source: Semi-dominant PHB alleles produce two leaf types on the same plant: partially radialized leaves with distal lamina and completely radialized (adaxialized) leaves (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is an established phenotype of phb-1d mutants shown in Figure 3I.

claim: In 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA phb-1d/+ plants, leaves with distal lamina exhibited ectopic marginal growth while radialized leaves did not.
source: In 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA phb-1d/+ plants, leaves with distal lamina exhibited ectopic marginal growth while radialized leaves did not, demonstrating that ongoing marginal growth first requires the juxtaposition of polarity factors (Figure 3J, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phenotypic data shown in Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ongoing marginal growth first requires the juxtaposition of polarity factors.
source: In 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA phb-1d/+ plants, leaves with distal lamina exhibited ectopic marginal growth while radialized leaves did not, demonstrating that ongoing marginal growth first requires the juxtaposition of polarity factors (Figure 3J, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that radialized leaves without polarity juxtaposition do not show marginal growth.

claim: PRS and WOX1 redundantly promote growth as an output of the abaxial/adaxial polarity program.
source: PRS and WOX1 redundantly promote growth as an output of the abaxial/adaxial polarity program (Nakata et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Nakata et al.'s work.

claim: prs wox1 double mutants suppressed the indeterminate marginal growth in 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants.
source: Notably, prs wox1 double mutants suppressed the indeterminate marginal growth in 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants (Figure 3K–L, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phenotypic data shown in Figure 3K–L and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The ongoing leaf margin growth is dependent on both the polarity program and the leaf-specific WOX genes.
source: Hence the ongoing leaf margin growth is dependent on both the polarity program and the leaf-specific WOX genes.
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic experiments showing requirements for both polarity factors and WOX genes.

claim: The abaxial surfaces of developing kan1 kan2 mutant leaves exhibit ectopic expression of PIN1, PRS and NGA1.
source: The abaxial surfaces of developing kan1 kan2 mutant leaves exhibit ectopic expression of PIN1, PRS and NGA1 (Figure 3M–P).
evidence: This is demonstrated by marker expression data shown in Figure 3M–P.

claim: Reducing both NGA and CIN-TCP activity in the kan1 kan2 background results in a striking proliferation of leaf tissue from the abaxial surface.
source: Reducing both NGA and CIN-TCP activity in the kan1 kan2 background results in a striking proliferation of leaf tissue from the abaxial surface (Figure 3Q, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phenotypic data shown in Figure 3Q and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutants of the adaxial factor ASYMMETRIC LEAVES2 (AS2) have patches of ectopic, adaxial PRS expression.
source: Similarly, reducing NGA and CIN-TCP activities in mutants of the adaxial factor ASYMMETRIC LEAVES2 (AS2), where patches of ectopic, adaxial PRS expression are observed, resulted in adaxial lamina proliferation (Figure 3R–U, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by marker expression and phenotypic data shown in Figure 3R–U and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Reducing NGA and CIN-TCP activities in as2 mutants resulted in adaxial lamina proliferation.
source: Similarly, reducing NGA and CIN-TCP activities in mutants of the adaxial factor ASYMMETRIC LEAVES2 (AS2), where patches of ectopic, adaxial PRS expression are observed, resulted in adaxial lamina proliferation (Figure 3R–U, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phenotypic data shown in Figure 3R–U and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ectopic abaxial expression of WOX1 in FIL:WOX1 plants results in abaxial outgrowths.
source: A shift in the marginal program with corresponding lamina outgrowths can also be achieved through direct manipulation of WOX1 expression, such as ectopic abaxial expression of WOX1 in FIL:WOX1 plants (Figure 4A–C) (Nakata et al., 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phenotypic data shown in Figure 4A–C and cited from Nakata et al.'s work.

claim: In FIL:WOX1 plants, PIN1 and NGA1 expression is detected in the abaxial outgrowths.
source: Here, as in kan1 kan2 mutant leaves, we detected PIN1 and NGA1 expression in the abaxial outgrowths.
evidence: This is demonstrated by marker expression data.

claim: The indeterminate cell proliferation and patterning of the leaf margin in 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants suggests it is self-organizing, a property of meristems.
source: The indeterminate cell proliferation and patterning of the leaf margin in 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants suggests it is self-organizing, a property of meristems, consistent with results demonstrating positive and negative feedbacks between PRS/WOX1 and adaxial/abaxial polarity factors (Nakata and Okada, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference from the observed patterns and cited feedback mechanisms.

claim: There are positive and negative feedbacks between PRS/WOX1 and adaxial/abaxial polarity factors.
source: The indeterminate cell proliferation and patterning of the leaf margin in 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants suggests it is self-organizing, a property of meristems, consistent with results demonstrating positive and negative feedbacks between PRS/WOX1 and adaxial/abaxial polarity factors (Nakata and Okada, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Nakata and Okada's work.

claim: The lack of marginal growth in radialized phb-1d/+ organs argues for a major role of the polarity factors in marginal positioning of a leaf meristem that requires the intervening activity of WOX genes.
source: The lack of marginal growth in radialized phb-1d/+ organs and its ectopic placement at discrete positions of the lamina when the adaxial/abaxial patterning is compromised argues for a major role of the polarity factors in marginal positioning of a leaf meristem that requires the intervening activity of WOX genes.
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic experiments with polarity mutants.

claim: A negative feedback loop between the marginally restricted meristem and NGA/CIN-TCP activities may lead to the ephemeral nature of this meristem.
source: In turn, a negative feedback loop between the marginally restricted meristem and NGA/CIN-TCP activities may lead to the ephemeral nature of this meristem.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed interactions.

claim: Leaves of FIL:WOX1 that are likely relieved from negative feedback regulation maintained a highly meristematic nature and failed to differentiate and expand when NGA and CIN-TCP activities were jointly reduced.
source: In agreement, leaves of FIL:WOX1 that are likely relieved from such feedback regulation, maintained a highly meristematic nature and failed to differentiate and expand when NGA and CIN-TCP activities were jointly reduced (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phenotypic data shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: The observation that loss of NGAs and CIN-TCPs results in indeterminate leaf margins suggests that the early wild-type leaf primordium has a meristem that acts during a brief developmental window and that is gradually restricted spatially.
source: The observation that loss of NGAs and CIN-TCPs results in indeterminate leaf margins suggests that the early wild-type leaf primordium has a meristem that acts during a brief developmental window and that is gradually restricted spatially (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: This interpretation is consistent with classical morphological and anatomical studies in which the definition of the marginal meristem was extended to include the entire meristematic leaf primordium at very early stages of leaf development.
source: This interpretation is consistent with classical morphological and anatomical studies in which the definition of the marginal meristem was extended to include the entire meristematic leaf primordium at very early stages of leaf development (Hagemann, 1970).
evidence: This is a comparison with historical literature.

claim: If a leaf primoridum is damaged or bifurcated at early stages, nearly complete regeneration of normal leaf morphology is possible.
source: If a leaf primoridum is damaged or bifurcated at this stage, nearly complete regeneration of normal leaf morphology is possible (Goebel, 1902; Figdor, 1906; Snow and Snow, 1941; Sachs, 1969).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple historical studies.

claim: As the meristematic regions become restricted to the margins or portions of the margins, damage or bifurcation of the leaf primordium results in progressively more limited regenerative capacity.
source: Subsequently, as the meristematic regions become restricted to the margins or portions of the margins, damage or bifurcation of the leaf primordium results in progressively more limited regenerative capacity (Snow and Snow, 1941; Sachs, 1969; Figdor, 1926).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple historical studies.

claim: Arabidopsis leaves are argued to possess a basal meristem that remains transiently active after leaf initiation before transitioning to petiole development — a process regulated by the BLADE-ON-PETIOLE (BOP) genes.
source: Arabidopsis leaves are argued to possess a basal meristem that remains transiently active after leaf initiation before transitioning to petiole development — a process regulated by the BLADE-ON-PETIOLE (BOP) genes (Hepworth et al., 2005; Ichihashi et al., 2011; Kuchen et al., 2012; Laux et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple studies.

claim: Early distal expression of CIN-TCP and NGA genes represses the meristem distally, but the lack of early proximal expression allows marginal persistence of the leaf meristem at the leaf base.
source: Our observations are consistent with early distal expression of CIN-TCP and NGA genes repressing the meristem distally, but the lack of early proximal expression allows marginal persistence of the leaf meristem at the leaf base, as reflected by PRS expression dynamics and leaf marginal cell differentiation along the proximo-distal axis (Nakata et al., 2012) (Figure 1P, Figure 1—figure supplements 6 and 8).
evidence: This is an inference from expression patterns and differentiation data.

claim: Whereas Arabidopsis leaves differentiate from tip to base, leaf differentiation in some other angiosperm species can proceed from base to tip.
source: Whereas Arabidopsis leaves differentiate from tip to base, leaf differentiation in some other angiosperm species can proceed from base to tip (Trécul 1853; Ikeuchi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from historical and recent studies.

claim: Variations in lateral organ growth within an individual and among species reflect differential maintenance of meristem activity along the marginal and proximo-distal axes.
source: We thus speculate that variations in lateral organ growth within an individual and among species reflect differential maintenance of meristem activity along the marginal and proximo-distal axes.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the findings.

claim: Lobe formation in many species relies on leaf-specific activity of class 1 KNOX (KNOX1) genes, which the simple leaves of Arabidopsis lack.
source: Remarkable diversity in leaf shape can arise from growth variation along the margin including leaf lobing. Lobe formation in many species relies on leaf-specific activity of class 1 KNOX (KNOX1) genes, which the simple leaves of Arabidopsis lack (Piazza et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Piazza et al.'s work.

claim: Lobes can be mimicked by ectopic KNOX1 expression in Arabidopsis leaves.
source: However, lobes can be mimicked by ectopic KNOX1 expression in Arabidopsis leaves.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: The radialized leaves of phb-1d/+ plants, a prs wox1 background and NGA1 over-expression, all suppresses the KNOX1-induced lobing phenotype.
source: The radialized leaves of phb-1d/+ plants, a prs wox1 background and NGA1 over-expression, all suppresses the KNOX1-induced lobing phenotype, indicating that an active marginal meristem is a prerequisite to respond to KNOX1 activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: An active marginal meristem is a prerequisite to respond to KNOX1 activity.
source: The radialized leaves of phb-1d/+ plants, a prs wox1 background and NGA1 over-expression, all suppresses the KNOX1-induced lobing phenotype, indicating that an active marginal meristem is a prerequisite to respond to KNOX1 activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic suppression experiments.

claim: Modulation in the marginal restriction of meristem activities can contribute to leaf shape diversity.
source: Thus modulation in the marginal restriction of meristem activities can contribute to leaf shape diversity.
evidence: This is an inference from the observations about KNOX1 activity and leaf shape.

claim: Cotyledons and floral organs are viewed as modified leaves.
source: Cotyledons and floral organs are viewed as modified leaves.
evidence: This is established knowledge in plant biology.

claim: In Arabidopsis, lack of a basally restricted meristem may distinguish cotyledons and floral organs from leaves in their response to reduced CIN-TCPs and NGA activity.
source: In Arabidopsis, lack of a basally restricted meristem may distinguish them from leaves in their response to reduced CIN-TCPs and NGA activity.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed differences in phenotypes.

claim: In cotyledons and floral organs, additional growth is confined to the distal region whereas in leaves the entire margin is affected.
source: In these organs, additional growth is confined to the distal region whereas in leaves the entire margin is affected (Figure 1A–B, Figure 1—figure supplements 3, 14 and 15).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phenotypic data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The observation that leaf tissue grows from cotyledon tips suggests a brief activity of a marginal meristem in cotyledons.
source: The observation that leaf tissue grows from cotyledon tips suggests a brief activity of a marginal meristem in cotyledons.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed cotyledon phenotypes.

claim: Prolongation of the marginal meristem activity likely uncouples growth from the embryonic cotyledon program, and therefore, cotyledons continue to grow the same way as leaves.
source: Prolongation of the marginal meristem activity likely uncouples growth from the embryonic cotyledon program, and therefore, cotyledons continue to grow the same way as leaves.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed phenotypes.

claim: The seed plant SAM exhibits two distinct organizational features: a tunica-corpus structure and cytohistological zonation.
source: The seed plant SAM exhibits two distinct organizational features. Firstly, SAMs feature a tunica-corpus structure in which cell divisions in the tunica are almost exclusively anticlinal (Schmidt, 1924). Secondly, the seed plant SAM exhibits cytohistological zonation that is correlated with functional zonation (Foster, 1938).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from historical studies.

claim: In the SAM tunica-corpus structure, cell divisions in the tunica are almost exclusively anticlinal.
source: Firstly, SAMs feature a tunica-corpus structure in which cell divisions in the tunica are almost exclusively anticlinal (Schmidt, 1924).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Schmidt's work.

claim: The central zone (CZ) of the SAM exhibits low rates of mitoses and acts to supply cells to the peripheral zone (PZ) and rib zone (RZ) where mitotic activity is high, and organogenesis occurs.
source: The central zone (CZ) exhibits low rates of mitoses and acts to supply cells to the peripheral zone (PZ) and rib zone (RZ) where mitotic activity is high, and organogenesis occurs (Steeves and Sussex, 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Steeves and Sussex's work.

claim: Cell lineage analyses of the SAM reveals that the majority of sectors observed do not extend to include the SAM, but rather are presumed to originate in derivatives of the peripheral/rib zones.
source: Consistent with these patterns of cell division, cell lineage analyses of the SAM reveals that the majority of sectors observed do not extend to include the SAM, but rather are presumed to originate in derivatives of the peripheral/rib zones (Dulieu, 1969; Jegla and Sussex, 1989; Furner and Pumfrey, 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple studies.

claim: Leaf meristems consist of distinct organizational zones: regions of low and high mitotic activity correspond to the classically defined 'marginal' and 'plate' meristems.
source: As with SAMs, leaf meristems can also be interpreted to consist of distinct organizational zones. Regions of low and high mitotic activity correspond to the classically defined 'marginal' and 'plate' meristems (Foster, 1936; Avery, 1933; Schüepp, 1926; Maksymowych and Wochok, 1969; Maksymowych and Erickson, 1960; Fuchs, 1966; Thomasson, 1970; Dubuc-Lebreux and Sattler, 1981; Jéune, 1981).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited historical studies.

claim: Cell lineage analyses reveal that the majority of sectors produced in developing leaves are derived from regions internal to the margins.
source: Consistent with these mitotic indices, cell lineage analyses reveal that the majority of sectors produced in developing leaves are derived from regions internal to the margins (Dulieu, 1968; Poethig and Sussex, 1985; Dolan and Poethig, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple studies.

claim: When marginal activity of the leaf meristem is extended, cells generated at the margins are displaced towards the center of the leaf, displaying a maturation gradient, similar to the PZ and RZ cells displaced from the CZ of the SAM.
source: While marginal activity of the leaf meristem in wild-type Arabidopsis may be brief, we show here that when extended, cells generated at the margins are displaced towards the center of the leaf, displaying a maturation gradient, similar to the PZ and RZ cells displaced from the CZ of the SAM.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the marking experiments and cell differentiation patterns in 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants.

claim: The CZ of the SAM is characterized by the expression of a WOX gene, WUSCHEL.
source: The CZ of the SAM is characterized by the expression of a WOX gene, WUSCHEL (Mayer et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Mayer et al.'s work.

claim: Loss-of-function WUS alleles generate a functional SAM, but the CZ fails to be maintained, leading to the eventual depletion of cells in the active PZ and RZ.
source: Loss-of-function WUS alleles generate a functional SAM, but the CZ fails to be maintained, leading to the eventual depletion of cells in the active PZ and RZ (Laux et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Laux et al.'s work.

claim: The leaf meristem exhibits WOX gene expression, whose function is required for continued leaf growth.
source: Similarly, the leaf meristem exhibits WOX gene expression, whose function is required for continued leaf growth, but leaves can initiate and grow for a while without marginal WOX expression (Nakata et al., 2012; Vandenbussche et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple studies.

claim: Leaves can initiate and grow for a while without marginal WOX expression.
source: Similarly, the leaf meristem exhibits WOX gene expression, whose function is required for continued leaf growth, but leaves can initiate and grow for a while without marginal WOX expression (Nakata et al., 2012; Vandenbussche et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple studies.

claim: The leaf marginal domain is organized into epidermal and sub-epidermal layers.
source: As with the SAM, the leaf marginal domain is also organized into epidermal and sub-epidermal layers.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: Analysis of periclinal chimeras revealed that the epidermal layers of the leaf are clonally related, whereas the mesophyll and vascular bundles are derived from subepidermal layers.
source: Analysis of periclinal chimeras revealed that the epidermal layers of the leaf are clonally related, whereas the mesophyll and vascular bundles are derived from subepidermal layers ([Foster, 1936; Avery, 1933; Baur, 1909] and references therein).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from historical studies.

claim: The lack of differentiation of leaf marginal cells in 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants is consistent with these cells remaining meristematic.
source: The lack of differentiation of leaf marginal cells in 35S:miR319a/35S:amiR-NGA plants is consistent with these cells remaining meristematic.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed cellular characteristics.

claim: The results are largely consistent with classical views of leaf development — that the leaf primordium is broadly meristematic at its inception, and that meristematic potential is subsequently restricted to the marginal regions.
source: Our results are largely consistent with classical views of leaf development — that the leaf primordium is broadly meristematic at its inception, and that meristematic potential is subsequently restricted to the marginal regions (Foster, 1936; Hagemann and Gleissberg, 1996; Jéune, 1981; Sachs, 1969).
evidence: This is a comparison with historical literature.

claim: The marginal and plate meristems represent two zones of a leaf meristem, analogous, or perhaps homologous, to the central and peripheral zones of the SAM.
source: In our view, the marginal and plate meristems represent two zones of a leaf meristem, analogous, or perhaps homologous, to the central and peripheral zones of the SAM.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the findings.

claim: The marginal restriction of the leaf meristem is in part maintained and guided by the same adaxial and abaxial factors that function in shoot and cambial meristems.
source: We suggest that the marginal restriction of the leaf meristem is in part maintained and guided by the same adaxial and abaxial factors that function in shoot and cambial meristems, and all three meristems are maintained by the activity of different WOX paralogs, suggesting the repeated use of a molecular module (Figure 4F) (Aichinger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic data and cited literature.

claim: All three meristems (leaf, shoot, and cambial) are maintained by the activity of different WOX paralogs, suggesting the repeated use of a molecular module.
source: We suggest that the marginal restriction of the leaf meristem is in part maintained and guided by the same adaxial and abaxial factors that function in shoot and cambial meristems, and all three meristems are maintained by the activity of different WOX paralogs, suggesting the repeated use of a molecular module (Figure 4F) (Aichinger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic data and cited literature.

claim: Sharing of genetic modules implies either common descent or co-option of modules to pattern novel structures.
source: Sharing of genetic modules implies either common descent or co-option of modules to pattern novel structures.
evidence: This is general evolutionary reasoning.

claim: Since seed plant leaves evolved from ancestral shoot systems, common descent is plausible.
source: Since seed plant leaves evolved from ancestral shoot systems, common descent is plausible.
evidence: This is reasoning based on evolutionary knowledge.

claim: The leaf meristem module has been modified from an ancestral shoot meristem module to include the leaf-specific WOX1 and PRS paralogs that arose in a common ancestor of seed plants.
source: In this scenario, the leaf meristem module has been modified from an ancestral shoot meristem module to include the leaf-specific WOX1 and PRS paralogs (Lin et al., 2013; Nardmann and Werr, 2013) that arose in a common ancestor of seed plants.
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference based on cited studies.

claim: Additional regulators such as the YABBY genes, which are instrumental in lamina growth and restrict activity of SAM factors, were integrated into the leaf program.
source: Additional regulators such as the YABBY genes, which are instrumental in lamina growth and restrict activity of SAM factors (Sarojam et al., 2010), and later acting factors limiting leaf meristem activity (i.e., CIN-TCP and NGA) were integrated into the leaf program.
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference based on cited studies.

claim: Later acting factors limiting leaf meristem activity (i.e., CIN-TCP and NGA) were integrated into the leaf program.
source: Additional regulators such as the YABBY genes, which are instrumental in lamina growth and restrict activity of SAM factors (Sarojam et al., 2010), and later acting factors limiting leaf meristem activity (i.e., CIN-TCP and NGA) were integrated into the leaf program.
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference from the study's findings.

claim: Growth suppressors modulating leaf meristem activity were recruited from genes of both ancient and recent origins — CIN-TCP genes are present in all land plants whereas NGA genes evolved recently, perhaps within seed plants.
source: Growth suppressors modulating leaf meristem activity were recruited from genes of both ancient and recent origins — CIN-TCP genes are present in all land plants (Navaud et al., 2007) whereas NGA genes evolved recently, perhaps within seed plants (Alvarez et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference based on cited phylogenetic studies.

claim: The leaf marginal meristem genetic program may have been derived via elaboration of an ancestral shoot program, reflecting the derivation of the leaf from a modified shoot.
source: Thus the leaf marginal meristem genetic program may have been derived via elaboration of an ancestral shoot program, reflecting the derivation of the leaf from a modified shoot.
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference from the findings.

claim: The identification of the genetic framework provides a unification of how the entire seed plant shoot system is built from apical, vascular, cambial, and leaf meristems that are mechanistically similar.
source: The identification of such genetic framework provides a unification of how the entire seed plant shoot system is built from apical, vascular, cambial, and leaf meristems that are mechanistically similar.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings about shared genetic modules.

claim: The evolution of seed plant leaves from an ancestral shoot system can be interpreted as evolving via the recruitment of regulatory mechanisms to suppress the morphogenetic potential of the leaf meristem.
source: The evolution of seed plant leaves from an ancestral shoot system can be interpreted as evolving via the recruitment of regulatory mechanisms to suppress the morphogenetic potential of the leaf meristem.
evidence: This is an evolutionary interpretation based on the findings.
